chunks: Motor poles and performance. The question: What are the poles of the motor? How can they impact performance?
Poles are the magnetic north and south regions on the rotor, arranged N, S, N, S around the rim.
The number of pole pairs decides how many electrical cycles happen in one turn of the shaft.
More poles give more torque at lower speed, but they require a faster electrical frequency for the same rpm (revolutions per minute).
Think of a bicycle in a low gear. Your legs spin the pedals many times for each turn of the wheel, and you push with more force.
More poles act like a lower gear inside the motor: for each shaft turn, the controller must cycle the current more times, and the motor gives more torque for its size.
The analogy has a limit: a real gear multiplies torque exactly, while extra poles help only through a better magnetic design, and add losses.
Same rotor diameter, different pole counts. With 2 poles one turn of the shaft is one electrical cycle; with 14 poles, one shaft turn is seven electrical cycles.
The stator fields and the Hall pattern repeat seven times per turn, so the rotor only needs to move 1/7 of a turn to advance one full electrical cycle.
Pole: one magnetic north or south region on the rotor. Pole pair ( p ): one north and one south pole together.
Electrical frequency: how many electrical cycles per second the controller drives, f equals p times rpm over 60 .
Electrical cycle: one full north-then-south pass of the rotor's magnets past a coil. The controller must drive one current cycle for each.
Cogging: a slight notchy feel as the rotor magnets are pulled toward the iron of the fixed part (stator).
A 14-pole motor has 14 / 2 = 7 pole pairs. At 30,000 rpm, the shaft turns 30,000 / 60 = 500 times per second. The electrical frequency is 7 times 500 = 3,500 hertz , or 3.
5 kilohertz. A 2-pole motor at the same speed has only 1 pair, so its electrical frequency is 500 hertz.
Higher electrical frequency means more switching loss and more heating in the motor's iron, but more torque from a compact motor.
That is the whole idea: poles trade torque against electrical frequency.
"Poles are the permanent-magnet poles on the rotor; p pole pairs means p electrical cycles per revolution, so f e equals p times rpm over 60 .
More poles gives more torque at lower speed for the same size, thinner back-iron, finer Hall resolution and, with the right slot count, less cogging.
The cost is a higher electrical frequency for the same rpm, which raises iron and switching losses and demands a faster controller.
Few poles suit very high speed; many poles suit gimbals, drones and direct drive."
